Header: Xylotrechus quadripes Coffee stem borer, white stem borer

Prevention: The coffee stem borer is a beetle which can fly.
Damage is caused by larvae which bore into the wood.
Use clean planting material which has been screened for coffee stem borer.
Remove and burn volunteer coffee plants from previous season in case they host the borer.
Don’t plant coffee trees with twisted taproots since they tend to be weak and more susceptible to coffee stem borer.
Remove the loose scaly bark of the main stem and thick primaries.
Smooth their surfaces by using a jute sack, coir glove or rough cloth before the period of borer flight activity to reduce the cracks and crevices in which the eggs are deposited.
Then, paste a mixture of red soil and fresh cow dung on the stem.
Spray 10% lime (i.e. spray lime at 10kg in 100 litres of water along with 100ml of a binder e.g.
DDL) on the main stem and thick primaries before the flight period.
Maintain optimum shade and soil moisture in the coffee orchard.
The borer is more active in the sunshine.
Monitoring: Adult: black and white striped pattern on wing cases/on its back slender, body 1-2 cm long
Larvae: white, front of head and mandibles are dark brown/ black, body about 2.5 cm long.
Feed on corky tissue just under the bark.
Later, they mine into the heartwood and sometimes the roots.
Frass on the ground which looks like sawdust.
Wilting and yellowing of leaves and dead branches which easily snap off.
Affected branches tend to be between ground level and 1 m up the stem.
Ridges on the main stem and thick primary stems.
Zigzag tunnels in woody tissue, on the upper part of branches (more exposed to sunlight), containing frass.
Holes in stems and branches, about 4-7 mm wide, where adults have emerged (exit holes).
Young plants are more likely to be killed by an infestation than older plants.
Use a coffee white stem borer pheromone trap, i.e. cross-vane pheromone trap, to catch female beetle during flight periods.
The traps should be spaced out in the form of a grid of 25 traps each with a spacing of 20 m between traps.
Take action when 5% of crop is affected.
Direct Control: An integrated pest management approach is needed to effectively manage this pest (use a combination of multiple prevention and control methods)
Paste or spray neem extract on the main stem and primary branches twice a year, using extract from seeds if possible (extract from leaves is less effective).
It should be applied at the beginning of the season
Spray the main stem and primary branches with 10% lime at a rate of 10 kgs in 100 litres of water.
Prune and uproot the infested plants and destroy by burning
